For a couple of years I worked in a VA hospital in the ER. I'm not medically trained - I was the night administrator, so I handled all the calls... records... those sorts of things. One night my partner and I were working the night shift and it was freezing outside. Middle of winter, northern latitude, snow and ice everywhere, pitch black, the whole nine. Some time after we had taken over from the 2nd shift I got a call from the cop on duty.

Cop: "Hey, Orange, I'm in the parking lot by Building 44, can you send [head nurse] out here with a blanket?"

Me: "Sure thing [cop]. Standby one." I was starting to page the head nurse when I got another call from the cop.

Cop: "Orange, better make that a Code Blue!"

I hate it when that happens. A Code Blue is when somebody needs the crash cart. Everybody drops everything they're doing a converges on the patient. I called the code blue over all the emergency channels... and immediately started getting calls from everybody asking me, "Where's Building 44?"

I directed everyone to the parking lot between two buildings, which is where the patient was - apparently - lying in the snow. In the middle of the night. Wearing nothing but his pajama bottoms (not even shoes).

And I waited. And I waited. And I waited some more. I was getting mystified by all that, because the guy was only about 100 yards from the ER. If it had been daylight I could have seen him. Then I got another call over the radio, "Orange, we need you to send an ambulance."

Say what?

Okay, I didn't say that, but I definitely thought it. The hospital didn't have its own ambulance, but the local ambulance was nearby, so I called 9-1-1 and told them what I needed. They arrived within about two minutes and I could see their lights out the front door. They were that close - why didn't they just use the gurney?

And I waited some more.

A few minutes later the ambulance pulled into the bay and I realized what the problem was: the guy was ENORMOUS. Probably 450 pounds.

THAT'S why they didn't just put him on the gurney and drag him to the ER... all nine people on the crash crew combined couldn't lift him and drag the gurney through the snow. They needed the burly guys on the ambulance crew, plus the ambulance itself to move him 100 yards.

Slowly the story trickled out. He had been admitted for breathing problems during the second shift, and some time during the night he had decided to go out to the loading dock to stand in the freezing winter air and smoke. He knew the ward nurses wouldn't let him do that, so he sneaked out. Once he got outside (behind the hospital) the door locked behind him. There he was, with a breathing problem so severe he had been admitted to the hospital, smoking outside in the freezing cold wearing nothing but paper-thin pajama bottoms, and now stuck on a loading dock while nobody knew he was missing. Since the only door that's unlocked at night is the ER, he had to walk barefoot through the snow all the way around the hospital to get back in. He ditched his IV pole (yeah... he was still plugged in to his IV) after about 100 yards, but he was still about 100 yards short of the ER when he collapsed, which is where the cop found him.

Despite the fact that the attending physician was our top cardiac specialist, the guy didn't survive, and after about 45 minutes of working on him the doctor pronounced him dead. I hadn't been paying much attention to other things, but out of the corner of my eye I had noticed a woman meandering around the hallway near the ER. I didn't think anything of it because she never came to the window to talk to me (she's going to be important in a minute).

Not five minutes later an older guy came in with chest pains, which means I had to go fetch his records while the nurse did her thing. My partner on admin duty that night was a crusty old dude who wanted to go out to the ambulance bay to smoke, and over his shoulder he said (loudly), "Don't worry about the dead guy. Take care of this guy." (Which I was going to do anyway, of course.) That's when I heard it... the female voice from the hallway...

"Well I'm the dead guy's fiance..."

OH CRAP! Well... that takes care of the death notification, I guess.

The guy's family tried to raise a stink about it, but it didn't go anywhere, since he had broken hospital rules and basically died of stupidity.
